I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

vignette: Kamal had always been a dancer at heart. Growing up in Baghdad, he would often sneak away from his parents' watchful eyes to watch videos of Michael Jackson and practice his moves in secret. As he grew older, dance became not just a passion but an escape - a way to express himself freely amidst the turmoil that surrounded him. When war broke out, Kamal's love for dance only intensified; it was a reminder of the beauty and joy that still existed, even as bombs rained down on his city. One fateful day, while walking home from rehearsal, Kamal found himself caught in the midst of a brutal firefight between rival factions. He remembers the deafening sounds of gunfire and screams, the acrid smell of smoke and earth filling his lungs. As he cowered behind a nearby wall, he watched in horror as a young boy - no more than ten years old - was gunned down just feet away from him. The image of that child's lifeless body, the sound of his mother's anguished wails, and the scent of damp earth where the boy lay would forever be seared into Kamal's memory. In the months following that fateful day, Kamal began to notice changes within himself. He felt numb, as if a part of him had been extinguished. The music he once loved now seemed hollow, the dance moves that used to bring him such joy now feeling forced and artificial. He would often catch himself standing still, lost in thought, as the sounds of everyday life - car horns, laughter, even the rustling of leaves - transported him back to that terrible moment. Even the simple act of walking through his neighborhood became an ordeal. The smell of freshly turned soil or the sweet scent of blooming jasmine would instantly evoke memories of that boy's lifeless body, and Kamal would find himself frantically scanning the area for signs of danger. At home, he began to avoid conversations with his wife about their future - about starting a family, building a new life together. It was as if he had lost faith not just in humanity but in the very concept of hope itself. Kamal became increasingly withdrawn, struggling to connect with those around him. He felt like an outsider, as though others could see the trauma etched on his face - that they knew exactly what had happened to him simply by looking at him. His wife would try to reassure him, but even her loving touch made him feel vulnerable, exposed. As a dancer, Kamal's body had always been his instrument, his source of expression and strength. But now it felt like a liability, a constant reminder of the fragility of life. He stopped performing, unable to bear the thought of being on stage, vulnerable and exposed before an audience. His absence from the dance scene didn't go unnoticed; old friends and colleagues would reach out, asking when he'd return to the stage. Kamal would respond with vague promises, but in truth, he felt like a part of him had died - that the spark within him had been extinguished forever. It was only when his wife sat him down, her eyes filled with tears, and said "Kamal, I feel like I'm losing you" that he realized just how far he'd drifted from the world around him. He saw the pain in her eyes, felt the weight of his own isolation, and knew that he needed help - not just for himself but for those who loved him. It was this realization that finally brought Kamal to seek therapy, hoping against hope that somehow, someway, he might rediscover the spark within himself, and learn to dance once more.
